headline: Honda: half-year profit up 66% as motorcycles earn ¥439 billion, but the car business still loses money and the forecast implies a weak second half
takeaway: Operating profit for the six months to September rose 48% to ¥648.7 billion and net profit 66% to ¥516.8 billion. Motorcycles earned a 19% margin while cars made a small loss, and Honda’s full-year forecast of ¥500 billion net profit is below what it has already earned. The ADRs slipped 1%.
results: Honda Motor reported sales revenue of ¥12.04 trillion for the six months ended September 30, up 13.2%. Operating profit rose 48.1% to ¥648.7 billion, profit before tax 40.5% to ¥740.9 billion and profit attributable to shareholders 65.7% to ¥516.8 billion, or ¥132.75 a share against ¥76.30 a year earlier.

By segment, the motorcycle business earned ¥439.1 billion on revenue of ¥2.27 trillion, a 19% margin, up from ¥368.3 billion. The automobile business lost ¥5.8 billion on revenue of ¥7.68 trillion, a big improvement on the ¥73.1 billion loss a year earlier. Financial services earned ¥211.0 billion, up from ¥143.2 billion.

Comprehensive income fell 21.7% to ¥382.7 billion. Capital spending in the automobile business more than tripled to ¥820.6 billion. The interim dividend was held at ¥35, with ¥70 forecast for the year.
mgmt: Honda revised its forecast for the year to March 2027 and now expects sales revenue of ¥24.4 trillion, up 11.9%, operating profit of ¥780 billion, profit before tax of ¥790 billion and profit attributable to shareholders of ¥500 billion, or ¥128.44 a share. That full-year net profit figure is below the ¥516.8 billion already earned in the first half.

The release reiterates the background: in the year to March 2026 Honda cancelled the development and launch of certain electric-vehicle models after reassessing its electrification strategy, recognising impairments and provisions in cost of sales, administrative expenses and research and development.
view: Honda is really two companies sharing a badge. One is the world’s largest motorcycle maker, selling some 20 million bikes a year in India, Indonesia, Vietnam and Brazil at margins close to 20% — a superb business that most investors forget about. The other is a mid-sized global carmaker that has spent two years caught between the cost of its electric-vehicle plans, US tariffs on Japanese-built cars and fierce competition from Chinese brands in Asia. This half-year confirms the pattern: the motorcycles and the finance arm earned all of the profit, and the cars roughly broke even.

The forecast is the puzzle. Guiding to ¥500 billion of net profit after earning ¥517 billion in six months implies the second half will be at break-even or slightly loss-making. The release does not spell out why, which usually means management is building in room for tariffs, further restructuring or EV-related costs that it does not want to quantify. Japanese managements are habitually conservative, and Honda has beaten its own guidance before, but a forecast that implies a profitless second half is a signal the car business is not yet fixed.

The bull case is that the market already prices Honda as if the car business were worth nothing: the motorcycle unit alone, valued like a premium two-wheeler peer, could justify much of the market capitalisation, and the company has been buying back stock aggressively since the collapsed merger talks with Nissan. The bear case is that the car business keeps absorbing the motorcycle profits through heavy capital spending — up threefold this half — with no clear path back to a mid-single-digit margin. Until the car division shows sustained profit, Honda will keep trading like a cheap carmaker rather than a quality motorcycle franchise.
watch: Watch automobile segment profit in the third quarter, any explanation of the conservative full-year forecast, the effect of US tariffs on Japan- and Mexico-built cars, and the pace of share buybacks.
